extracted.intended_audience: Lutheran pastors, church leaders, and denominational planners (early-20th-century New York context)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and practical guidance on language policy, membership classes and admission practices, confirmation and baptismal practice, pastoral care, and religious education for Lutheran congregations (with historical and doctrinal rationale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of ministry (English vs. other tongues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing, then, that Anglicization is inevitable, why should we not cut the Gordian knot, and conduct our ministry wholly in the English language? ... Some of the languages at present used in our church services may be of negligible importance. ... It is a different matter, however, when we come to High German, or, properly speaking, New High German ... This is a language which we could not lose if we would, and would not if we could.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh philological affinity, congregational needs, and generational assimilation: Low German and Scandinavian groups easily substitute English; Slovak, Magyar, Finnish, Lettish, Esthonian and Lithuanian have restricted future use. Preserve High German because of its indispensability to scholarship, literature (Goethe, Schiller), and Lutheran devotional resources; maintain bilingual ministry where helpful (e.g., Concordia Seminary expectation). Do not 'exterminate' minority languages; cultivate acquaintance and retain languages that enrich church life. Recognize Public School and Sunday School roles in assimilation; avoid blanket monolingualism that severs access to doctrinal/literary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classes of members are recognized in our churches: 1, Those who have been baptized. 2, Those who have been confirmed-that is, those who after the prescribed course of instruction and examination have been admitted to the communion. 3, Communicants-that is, those who are in active fellowship with the church in the use of the word and the sacrament. ... There is a fourth class ... the class of lapsed Lutherans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinct categories (baptized, confirmed, communicants) for ecclesiastical practice and statistics; separately acknowledge lapsed members who have slipped from active connection. Note civic/corporate voting qualifications are state-regulated and separate from spiritual membership categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for admission to membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretically we enter the church through baptism. Practically, for most Lutherans, confirmation is the door of admission. ... From this it seems that 'Missouri' is the only body that emphasizes the interna virtus. The others place the emphasis upon conformity with certain outward forms and requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission criteria may include baptism, confirmation after instruction/examination, acceptance of confessional documents, leading a Christian life, and obedience to constitution/regulations. Be aware of synodical variation (some emphasize inward regeneration, others external conformity). Keep admission practices consistent with both confessional principles and actual congregational usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation practice and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Their object in catechization and confirmation was conversion. ... We are not advocating extravagant ideas of conversion, or requiring a religious experience from children of fourteen years which in the nature of the case they cannot have. ... Does confirmation mean a family party, or mark the time to leave school, or has it something to do with baptism? These are rocks of offense which must be cleared out of the way if the Church is to be restored to health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat confirmation as the result of genuine catechization aiming at spiritual formation (regressus ad baptismum), not merely a public exhibition or social rite. Provide adequate preparation (more than the typical six months), emphasize conversion realities appropriate to age, and align confirmation practice with baptismal theology. Avoid reducing confirmation to a family party or school milestone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-confirmation interview and fitness examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the questions proposed to the pastors were the following: 1. Do you have a personal interview with each candidate prior to confirmation with the view of ascertaining his fitness for the act? 2. Do you at that interview inquire as to the candidate's repentance, faith, conversion, new life? 3. Is the confirmation of the candidate dependent upon the satisfactory result of this examination?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct individual interviews ('unter vier Augen') to ascertain genuine repentance, faith, and new life. Make confirmation dependent, where appropriate, on satisfactory individual examination rather than mere public/group testing. Anti-pattern: reliance solely on public examination or no personal enquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baptismal practice and qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as we practice the Winkeltaufe and baptize indiscriminately the children of people who give us no guarantee that the children will be brought up in the Christian faith, so long as the Church fails to recognize her obligation to these baptized children ... we have no right to place such an emphasis upon baptismal regeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconsider indiscriminate infant baptism (Winkeltaufe) where there is no guarantee of Christian upbringing; consider whether to baptize children of those who have abandoned the faith. Ensure baptismal practice is followed by sustained pastoral/catechetical care; avoid 'baptize and let them run' mentality. Reform confirmation practice in tandem with baptismal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral care and the confessional (care of souls)
rubrics_metrics.description: The care of souls cannot be performed in bulk, it is the care of a soul. ... Instead of it we have a hybrid combination of Lutheran doctrine and Reformed practice, and we distribute our absolution ore rotundo over mixed congregations on Sunday mornings and at the Preparatory Service. But the real confession we seldom hear and a valid absolution therefore we cannot pronounce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize individual pastoral attention, genuine confession, and properly pronounced absolution. Avoid mass or 'bulk' pastoral practices (public-only examination, general absolution) that forfeit meaningful pastoral relationships and valid pastoral care. Re-establish private pastoral relationships (confessor/beichvater) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rite of initiation and formal admission procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission to membership should take place by vote of the congregation or at least of the Church Council. There should likewise be some rite of initiation. In the case of adults who come from other congregations it need not and should not be a confirmation service, but it should at least be a public introduction of the candidate into the fellowship of the congregation with which he desires to become identified. (Matthew 10, 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure formal admission processes: congregational or council vote, a public rite of initiation, and distinct procedures for adults (public introduction rather than confirmation). Maintain clear records and differentiation between occasional communicants and actual members for statistics and pastoral oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between visible and invisible Church (Lutheran via media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the Romanists regard the Church as essentially visible, the Reformed, as essentially invisible, while Lutherans hold that she is both. The invisible Church is contained within the visible just as the soul is contained within the body. The Church is not merely a congregation of believers, but also an institution for the promotion of the Kingdom of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a theological balance: uphold the inward spiritual reality (faith, Holy Spirit) while preserving visible marks (preaching of the pure Gospel and administration of the sacraments). Guard against slipping toward Roman externalism (over-institutionalism) or Reformed hyper-spiritualism (denial of ordinances' importance). Use confessions and practice to keep the via media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church's pedagogic duty and role in nurture
rubrics_metrics.description: In this relation the Church is not only the product, but also the organ of the Holy Ghost. It is her duty to nourish the life of its members (parturit et alit), and to spread the blessings of the Church to others. ... As a national church, her relations to the people were different ... Her pedagogic duty is pointed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and enact the Church's duty to educate and nurture believers: systematic catechesis, ongoing instruction, and pastoral formation. The Church should function as spiritual 'mother' and training force, responsible for continuous care and edification of members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forces shaping church practice (doctrine, tradition, environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of our churches is a resultant mainly of three forces: 1. Doctrine, defined in the Confessions... 2. Tradition, from the civil and social arrangements of the national churches... 3. Environment. Consciously or unconsciously we are influenced by the practice of neighboring denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or reforming practice, analyze influences from doctrine, inherited tradition, and local environment. Test practices against historic principles and Scripture; be aware that 'the way we have always been doing' may perpetuate unsound practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious education (weekday instruction vs. Sunday School)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically and doctrinally the Lutheran Church is committed to week-day instruction in religion. ... The Sunday School ... with but half an hour a week for instruction, even the best of teachers could not expect important results. ... The Sunday School has untold possibilities of usefulness. But all its merits and advantages cannot close our eyes to the fact that it does not and cannot meet the chief requirement of the Christian school, the systematic preparation of all the children for the duties of church membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide systematic, graded, weekday religious instruction (parochial or other) to prepare children for church membership; treat Sunday School as a valuable supplement but not sufficient for comprehensive formation. Ensure instruction is accessible to all children (not merely voluntary attendance) and integrated with life and school experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of parochial schools and comprehensive programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing this obligation some of our churches maintain the Parochial School.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider parochial schools or similar weekday programs as means to fulfill the Church's responsibility for comprehensive religious education; they help overcome Sunday School's limitations and reach children who might otherwise receive no instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for multilingual ministers in polyglot contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Concordia Seminary in St. Louis, founded by Dr. Walther and the Germans of Missouri, numbers 344 students. Candidates for graduation must be able to minister in at least two languages. In a polyglot church such as ours this would seem to be a policy worthy of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train and require clergy competent in multiple languages where congregations are polyglot, to serve immigrant and bilingual populations effectively and to preserve access to liturgy and literature in original tongues when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess actual practice, not only constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: But we cannot always judge from the printed constitution. To bring the information up to date, and to ascertain the actual usage of the churches, the author obtained from forty pastors of this city an account of their practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming policy or evaluating congregations, survey actual pastoral practice and lived congregational habits in addition to stated constitutional requirements; expect variance between printed rules and praxis and adjust reforms accordingly.
